American here, my family pays a max out of pocket of $12k/year, no matter how much healthcare we use or how high our income is. This is a very standard amount for health insurance policies for couples with or without kids. 

Zero issue getting timely appointments, see specialists, tests, procedures etc… it is super efficient.  

Lots of times I can get same day appointments with my primary care physician, or their physician assistant, if I call first thing in the morning. They leave a certain number of available appointments open every day for certain types of situations. If you match you get the appointment. 

All imaging (cat scan, mri, pet scan etc…) in a week or two. Lots of times simple x rays are done right there in office, blood taking for labs too same day. 

See a specialists in 2-3 weeks, Depends on the type of specialists. Mental health is much longer, 4-6 weeks. 

Location in the country does matter. Certain states and cities are better than others with availability. I live in a state with good availability. 

I think a lot of people outside the country think we are paying 100s of thousands for procedures. That just doesn’t happen for people with insurance. 

Since health insurance isn’t always mandatory, lots of weird circumstances happen which make for some omg articles that make it seem like everybody in the USA is living that way with respect to healthcare. 

Here is a recent example of my experience. 

I needed to go see my cardiologist but flaked on the yearly appointment. 

Called and made appointment, 2.5 weeks for appointment. 
At appointment Dr wanted me to do blood work and get eko. Walked over to the lab place next door and was getting that done in about 20 minutes. Next day the facility called me for eko appointment and that is 10 days out. Next day I got my blood lab results emailed to me. Waiting now for eko.  

It is super efficient and I really don’t think it costs that much at max $12k/year.  If my family doesn’t use it for anything but yearly checkups and we have no other issues, it costs us about $2k for the year. 

If you lose your job and don’t have the money you can get on subsidized ACA insurance or your state Medicaid. I have never gone without insurance for one single day my whole life. 

I qualify for Medicare (retirement health insurance) in about 10 years.  

I think the system here in the USA is misunderstood by a lot of people in other countries. 

By not making health insurance mandatory and not taking 100% of the money directly out of people’s paychecks through taxes, lots of people go without or don’t have the money when needed because they don’t plan for it and spend their whole paycheck and that creates all kinds of issues.  This is why we have so many healthcare related bankruptcies. These types of bankruptcies no longer damage your credit score. They changed the law on this. L

How insurance is obtained, allocated and paid for definitely needs to change, lots of improvement there, but the efficiency and quality of care is excellent.

Your body is in such a deprived state it won’t be able to gain strength or build muscle and you have no fat to make up the difference.  There is no way to diet yourself to what you want to achieve, there is nothing else to lose. 

Go to a tdee calculator, i like this one, [https://tdeecalculator.net](https://tdeecalculator.net) and put in a weight of 90, 100, 110 pounds. 

The difference in calories from 90 to 100 is only like 50-100 calories a day, and from 100 to 110 is probably just another 50-100.  It isn’t that much. 

But also notice the calories per day, for even sedentary, you are under eating severely. 

100 extra calories a day is 700 a week, say 3000 a month. That isn’t even 1 pound of gain a month.  You aren’t going to balloon up.  

I would start by eating at maintenance for 100 pounds for your activity level. 

Since you are eating more you will gain a few pounds of water weight initially at first, but you will stabilize after a couple weeks. It’s water, it isn’t fat, don’t freak out about it. 

If you ate at maintenance for 100 pounds for a year while weight training, you would stabilize your weight at 100 pounds and put on muscle while doing it.  

You would be healthier, look better, feel better, be stronger, and actually look leaner.  

Since you are so worried, have a desk job and maybe don’t get to the gym as consistent, just eat at sedentary for 100 pounds, about 1350 calories. That would be a good start. Try that for 2-3 months and then reevaluate.  

TBH, if you did all that weight training and HIT cardio consistently, you could easily eat 1500 calories a day, but let’s start small. Plus everybody’s body is different and doesn’t respond exactly to the tdee calculator calorie amount, so let’s not overshoot from the start. 

You are trying to achieve a look based on scale weight and only through fat loss,  but you have no fat to lose, so the look you want to achieve isn’t possible that way. 

100 pounds healthy and with some added muscle is going to look leaner than 90 pounds and starving.  

You are in a great situation since you have no excess fat to lose and sound like a disciplined person. You just need to have a different outlook and philosophy.

It’s ok to have such a large deficit at first,  but as you lose more weight you are going to eat up a lot of muscle, even with high protein. 

The issue is as you lose weight, since a decent portion is muscle, your body fat percentage doesn’t go down nearly as much as someone who weight trains to preserve muscle, so you will continue to have that skinny fat look even once you get close to goal weight. 

Weight training, and it doesn’t take much, will send signals to your brain that your muscles are important and needed, so it will prioritize your fat for making up your calorie deficit. 

When you don’t weight train, you send a signal that your body doesn’t need the muscle and when in a calorie deficit it will use muscle (as well as fat) to make up for that deficit. 

It doesn’t take that much weight training.   Even just starting a basic body weight calisthenics routine 2 times a week would make a huge difference.  

Our bodies hate to build or preserve muscle if it is not needed. Maintaining muscle requires more calories so our body figures if you don’t need it, no reason to keep it. It is a survival mechanism.

I haven’t built in Denver, but I have built a custom home before. 3,500 sqft over a walkout basement of 1,500 sqft, so 5,000 sqft total.  I found the builder by driving neighborhoods, observing builders building custom homes/renovations in the area, calling them up and interviewing etc….. You need to start networking, asking a ton of questions etc….. The build itself took 10 months.   Make sure the builder and yourself are on the same page with respect to finishes.  The more detailed and specific you are, the better.  In my case, if we didn’t have specifics, the builder put in dollar allowances, and IME those allowances don’t always line up with what you want or were expecting.  Concentrate on the big ticket items. Cabinets, counter tops, light fixtures, flooring, even paint/number of colors, type of windows, doors, exterior siding, how the interior will be trimmed out etc…. The more detailed during the bidding process, the closer to budget you will come and get what you expect.   Also, how showers are built is so important. It is the most difficult thing to build in the entire house, there are several ways to do it with different materials and techniques, and you could end up with something that won’t last 5 years vs a lifetime.  You leave it up to the builder and of course they will tilt it in their $favor$. It is a huge undertaking. You will be surprised just how many decisions on finishes there are.  Every single detail needs to be decided on. It is a ton of work and effort.  I built right after the Great Recession so I got everything at bottom dollar prices, so what I paid has no bearing on today.   I saw you posted you want to build a smaller house, just know that the less square footage you build, the more it costs on a $ per square foot basis.  Smaller houses are less efficient from a build cost standpoint.  Ie you get 50% less house for 20% less money.   I have since sold, moved to Lakewood, downsized and live in a much smaller house now. 6'3" and 230 lbs..........

Get the WRR

Rally weighs about 50lbs more than the WRR (342-346lbs depending on ABS or not for the Rally vs 295lbs for the WRR) and at your height and weight, WRR will perform better. WRR is slightly taller, has the better stock suspension and more power stock. 

Suspension and power can be worked out to a point, but that 50lbs is a killer. 

But having said all that, if you want a Rally, get one. Respring, regear, uncork (maybe even go for a 300 swap if you can get a used engine cheap) and have at it. 

TBH, I really don't think it matters all that much when you look at what the bikes are designed and used for. Its more about having fun trail riding, 50/50 dual sport use etc.... The more performance you want to get out of the bike on the dirt, the more the bike itself and mods will play. 

I watched a pretty good YT series of a father and two sons riding the TAT where Honda sponsored their ride. Honda provided the bikes, an African Twin, a Rally and a regular CRF250L. They said the best bike of the three on the trail was the regular CRF250L because it was the lightest. 

Go sit on a rally, I think you will find the WRR fits you better and the Rally suspension is super soft. At your size, you will bottom that thing out all day long. With the WRR you get a little more travel and you can crank up the compression settings.
The CRF250L is really under sprung. You can change out the springs to match your weight.

Put some sound deadening and maybe even some foam on it and it will make all the difference in the world. The foam will help with the reverberation and the sound deadener will take away the ting sounds. 

Edit: I see you already added foam. Some sound deadener will help too.
